metadata.title: Developing measures of engagement in PISA (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report uses published PISA microdata for PISA 2018, 2015, and 2012, and it applies standard PISA practice for uncertainty estimation under the complex survey design. In the analysis section, the authors state that estimated standard errors account for the complex design of PISA, implying the use of PISA’s replicate/variance estimation approach even though specific weight variable names are not provided in the excerpt. The study excludes the Une Heure (UH) booklet and, for questionnaire-based non-response, excludes students with non-response rates greater than 0.95, which changes the analytic sample composition. Because the paper is not an ML prediction study and does not report a model-based weighting strategy beyond complex-design standard errors, readers should rely on the PISA-provided variance estimation and any associated sampling weights in the underlying PISA datasets when reproducing the results.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report does not describe a specific missing-data handling method for the analytic models (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation) beyond explicit exclusions for questionnaire non-response rates and the construction rules for indices. Because the study relies on PISA background questionnaire responses and test response-time information, missingness is handled partly through indicator construction and targeted exclusions rather than a single, clearly documented imputation/deletion protocol. This constitutes a reporting gap for missing-data handling details needed for full reproducibility.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses use published PISA data (students’ responses and response times on the cognitive assessment, plus responses to the international student questionnaire; national optional questionnaires excluded). Students who took the Une Heure (UH) booklet are excluded to avoid confounding due to reduced testing time. For questionnaire-based non-response, students with non-response rates greater than 0.95 are excluded. For the performance-decline index, the authors estimate a random-coefficients model using an item-level dataset reconstructed for PISA 2018’s multi-stage adaptive design; performance decline is excluded from the regression predicting reading PVs because it draws on the same information as the reading performance measure.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper develops and evaluates multiple indicators of student disengagement in PISA, drawing on PISA 2018, 2015, and 2012. It computes seven disengagement measures spanning three information sources: self-reported effort (Effort thermometer; perseverance; work mastery), questionnaire-based behavioural indicators (non-response, non-differentiation, inconsistency), and test-based behavioural indicators (performance decline and rapid guessing based on response times). The study finds low consistency across most measures (often small or even negative correlations), while rapid guessing and questionnaire non-response show relatively stronger associations. Disengagement is systematically related to student characteristics: boys, socio-economically disadvantaged students, and students with an immigrant background show higher disengagement in most countries/economies. Disengagement is also associated with lower PISA reading performance (using reading plausible values), but the paper emphasizes that cross-sectional data prevent causal interpretation and that engagement-related measurement issues can threaten score comparability.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD working paper focused on constructing and validating engagement/disengagement indicators rather than training predictive ML models. As a result, there is no ML algorithm evaluation, no ML target-variable prediction pipeline, and no ML-based main findings table to populate. The extraction is therefore intentionally sparse for ML-specific fields (ml_techniques, main_findings, confounders_identified) because the paper’s core contribution is measurement development and descriptive/associational evaluation across PISA cycles.
